purpose: Provide Nairobi-specific context for realistic F-1 student-athlete mock visa interviews.
core_interview_areas: Why are you going to the United States?
Why did you choose this university?
Why did you choose this major or course?
How did you get your scholarship?
How many schools recruited you?
How many schools admitted you?
Why did you choose this school over the other schools?
Who is your sponsor?
What does your scholarship cover?
How will expenses not covered by the scholarship be paid?
What are your plans after graduation?
What sport or event do you compete in?
How were you recruited by the university?
When did you finish high school or your previous degree?
What have you been doing since finishing school?
What grades did you receive in high school or your previous studies?
How does your previous education connect to your new program?
What are your long-term academic, athletic and career goals?
Have you previously been refused a U.S. visa?
What has changed since your previous refusal?
What international travel have you completed before?
When do your classes start?
How will you catch up if your visa interview is close to or after your original class start date?
Has your university approved a late arrival or provided an extension letter?

questions: When did you finish high school?
What grade did you receive in high school?
What have you been doing since completing high school?
Why did you choose this program?
How does your academic background prepare you for this course?
What did you study during your undergraduate degree?
What have you been doing since graduation?
Why are you pursuing a master's degree now?
Why did you choose this master's program?
How does this master's program connect to your undergraduate degree?
If the new program is different from your previous degree, why are you changing fields?
How will this master's degree help your career after graduation?
How long has it been since you last attended school?
What have you been doing during that period?
Have you been working, training, competing or studying?
Why are you returning to school now?

school_start_date_intelligence.purpose: Test whether the athlete understands their university start date and any approved late-arrival arrangements.
interview_before_start_date: When do you plan to travel to the United States?
How soon after receiving your visa will you travel?
interview_very_close_to_start_date: Your classes begin very soon. How do you plan to arrive on time?
Have you communicated with your university about your visa interview date?
What arrangements have you made in case you arrive after classes begin?
interview_after_original_start_date: Your original class start date has already passed. Why are you still able to attend?
Has your university authorized you to arrive late?
What is your new approved arrival deadline?
How will you catch up with classes you may have missed?
Have your professors or university officials explained how you will catch up?
extension_letter_present: Who issued your late-arrival or extension letter?
What is the latest date your university has authorized you to arrive?
How will you catch up academically after arriving?
rules: Do not assume an extension letter exists unless it is recorded in the athlete profile.
Do not invent a new arrival date.
If an extension letter exists, use the actual approved date provided by the athlete.
Flag inconsistencies between the athlete's stated dates and their profile.

student_athlete_focus: Understand the relationship between athletics and academics.
Ask how the athlete earned or received the scholarship.
Ask how the university discovered or recruited the athlete.
Ask how many universities recruited the athlete.
Ask why the athlete selected this university over other opportunities.
Ask what the athletic scholarship covers.
Ask why this university is a good fit for the athlete's specific sport or event.
Check whether the athlete can clearly explain the chosen academic major.
Ask how the athlete plans to balance training, competition and academics.
Do not allow athletics to completely replace the academic purpose of the F-1 visa.
Ask about long-term academic and career goals.
Ask what the athlete plans to do after completing the degree.

university_choice: What other universities recruited or admitted you?
Why did you choose this university instead?
What specifically attracted you to this school's academic and athletic program?
scholarship: How did you get this scholarship?
Why did the university offer you the scholarship?
What exactly does your scholarship cover?
Is it an athletic scholarship, academic scholarship or a combination?
Who will pay for expenses not covered by the scholarship?
sponsor: How will your sponsor afford the remaining costs?
How much of your education is already covered by your scholarship?
major: Why did you choose this major?
What will you study in this program?
How does this course connect to your previous education?
How will this degree help you after graduation?
athletics: What event or sport do you compete in?
What are your personal best performances?
How did the university discover or recruit you?
Why is this university a good fit for your sport?
How will you balance athletics with your studies?
What are your long-term athletic goals?
high_school: When did you finish high school?
What have you been doing since you graduated?
How did you become eligible for admission to this university?
education_gap: What have you been doing since you finished school?
Why did you wait before continuing your education?
How has what you have been doing prepared you for university?
masters_applicant: What did you study during your undergraduate degree?
Why are you pursuing a master's degree?
What have you been doing since completing your undergraduate degree?
How will this master's degree contribute to your future career?
previous_refusal: What were you asked during that interview?
What has changed since your previous interview?
post_graduation: What do you plan to do after graduation?
Where do you plan to use this degree?
How will this degree be useful when you return home?
How do your academic and athletic goals fit into your long-term plans?
late_arrival: When were your classes originally scheduled to begin?
Why has your university allowed you to arrive later?
What is your approved arrival deadline?
How will you catch up academically?
Have you received an extension or late-arrival letter from the university?

rules: Do not ask every question in every interview.
Select questions based on the athlete's actual profile.
Ask high-school questions primarily to undergraduate applicants.
Ask undergraduate-history questions to master's applicants.
Ask education-gap questions when there is a meaningful gap in the athlete's education history.
Ask late-arrival questions when the interview date is close to or after the original university start date.
Ask refusal questions when the athlete has a previous refusal.
Ask funding follow-ups when the scholarship does not cover the full cost.
Use previous answers to generate natural follow-up questions.
Increase questioning when an answer is unclear, inconsistent or incomplete.
Avoid repeating questions the athlete has already answered clearly.

readiness_checks: University, major and scholarship information are consistent.
Student can clearly explain why they are going to the United States.
Student can explain why they selected the university.
Student can explain how they earned the scholarship.
Student can explain their previous education.
Student can explain any education gap.
Student can explain athletics without making athletics the only purpose of studying.
Student can explain their long-term academic, athletic and career goals.
Student understands their class start date.
If late arrival applies, the student can clearly explain the approved arrangement.
Previous refusal answers are consistent with the athlete's history.
Post-graduation plans are understandable and consistent.

observed_nairobi_patterns.status: Reviewed interview observations and preparation intelligence. These are not guaranteed embassy rules.
areas_seen_in_reports: Reason for traveling to the United States
Activities since high school or graduation
Number of universities recruiting the athlete

safety_rules: Never present interview patterns as official embassy rules.
Never coach the athlete to provide false information.
Never invent grades, scholarship amounts, sponsors, dates or university information.
Flag contradictions instead of inventing explanations.
Do not use officer race, ethnicity, gender or appearance to predict visa outcomes.
Readiness scores measure preparation only, not probability of visa approval.
A university extension or late-arrival letter should be treated as supporting information, not a guarantee of visa issuance.
